idiom_name: tokio mpsc channel + a dispatcher task spawning one task per message (std mpsc + worker threads for blocking code)
implementation_notes: Rust has no dispatcher object but the standard library supplies the queue: std::sync::mpsc's Sender/Receiver (or sync_channel for a bounded, blocking hand-off) with N std::thread workers is the hand-rolled form, and it is what blocking code should use. In async code the runtime is the performer pool: the official tokio tutorial's message-passing shape - a dedicated task owns the resource, other tasks send it commands over mpsc::channel(n), and it processes each message in order - is the dispatcher, with tokio::spawn(msg) per message as the fan-out form and a Semaphore for admission control. Choose tokio when the surrounding program is async (std/crossbeam channels block a thread and are not allowed inside async tasks), and the hand-rolled pool when you need per-message dispatch policy or cannot take a runtime.
pitfalls: std::sync::mpsc has a single Receiver that cannot be cloned: sharing it across worker threads requires Arc<Mutex<Receiver>>, and that mutex becomes a serialized dispatch step under load.
Blocking in an async task starves the runtime: blocking work must go to spawn_blocking or a dedicated thread pool, and std::sync::mpsc/crossbeam channels must not be awaited in async code.
Unbounded channels (mpsc::unbounded_channel) turn overload into memory growth with no back-pressure; the bounded channel is the one that makes senders wait.
Messages crossing tasks or threads must be Send + 'static, and dropping the Receiver makes every send fail with SendError - producers must handle that as the shutdown signal it is.
A panicking task does not kill the process, but a JoinHandle that is never awaited hides the panic and the message it was processing is lost.
